summary: Engadget's year-end review says 2023 in video games was shaped by consolidation, layoffs and unionization, which fed into one another. Microsoft closed its $69 billion Activision-Blizzard-King purchase while Sony and Tencent kept expanding, and more than 9,000 game workers lost jobs. Union progress, notably at ZeniMax, offered some worker protection, and the author warns that consolidation makes studios more vulnerable to mass cuts.
one_line: A review of 2023 in games: Microsoft's Activision deal, Sony and Tencent consolidation, over 9,000 layoffs, and growing unionization.
key_facts: Microsoft's purchase of Activision-Blizzard-King was approved on October 12, 2023 after nearly two years of regulatory hurdles, making it the world's third-largest video game studio by revenue.
The Activision deal was worth $69 billion; King's Candy Crush Saga has 238 million monthly active users and more than $20 billion in lifetime revenue.
Sony owns 21 development teams and has 12 live-service titles in production, on top of Bungie's Destiny franchise.
Tencent is bigger than both Sony and Microsoft by the article's account, and is the biggest investor in games, with stakes in Epic, Ubisoft and Roblox and full ownership of Riot Games.
An estimated 9,000+ video game workers were laid off in 2023, compared with just 1,000 in 2022 according to layoffstracker.com.
Embracer Group announced in June 2023 that a six-year, $2 billion funding deal had fallen through, then shut down Volition, Free Radical Design and Campfire Cabal; more than 900 people lost jobs.
Epic Games fired roughly 830 people, 16 percent of its staff; CEO Tim Sweeney said the company had been spending way more money than it earned.
Electronic Arts cut about 800 employees (6 percent) in March and an estimated 1,130 jobs in 2023 overall; Unity cut about 900 jobs across three rounds.
Sony cut 100 jobs at Bungie, which it bought for $3.6 billion in 2022; Microsoft cut 10,000 jobs across its businesses, including about 100 at 343 industries.
Netflix launched its Games division in 2021 and has bought four studios, including Night School and Spry Fox.
Microsoft hosts the industry's largest union, with more than 300 QA workers at ZeniMax Media, recognized in January 2023, with negotiations beginning in April.
In December, Microsoft said it would hire 77 contract workers as full-time employees under the ZeniMax Workers United-CWA union, with a pay raise, paid holidays, sick leave and a copy of Starfield.
Raven Software QA employees voted to unionize in May 2022, and Microsoft has vowed to respect organizing efforts at Activision-Blizzard-King.
